original_question: Let p(n) be the partition function, so that sum_{n>=0} p(n)x^n = product_{k>=1} (1 - x^k)^(-1). Define integers n_k by the power-product expansion sum_{n>=0} p(n)x^n = product_{k>=1} (1 + n_k x^k). Explore the arithmetic properties of the sequence (n_k). In particular, determine whether n(8k + 2), n(8k + 4), and n(8k + 6) are always negative while n(8k) is always positive for every k >= 1.
target_in_paper: Section 2, Problem 3, in the section titled "Power product expansion of the generating function for the partition function" (page 3).

The sequence should be indexed explicitly as (n_k)_{k>=1}, and the paper states that it is the unique sequence of integers with this property.
To avoid ambiguity, the sign conditions should be written with subscripts n_{8k+2}, n_{8k+4}, n_{8k+6}, and n_{8k}, rather than function notation like n(8k+2).
The nearby context in Section 2 records that n_k = 1 for odd k, so the nontrivial arithmetic behavior under discussion is concentrated on the even-indexed terms.
For maximal fidelity to the paper, the question should preserve the paper's framing: first, broadly explore arithmetic properties of (n_k); second, in particular, ask the displayed sign question.

The paper notes immediately after Problem 3 that the displayed sign question may be approachable using a recurrence given in reference [4]; this is context, not part of the statement, but it is part of the paper's intent and scope.
refined_question: Let p(n) be the classical partition function, characterized by sum_{n>=0} p(n)x^n = product_{m>=1} (1 - x^m)^(-1). In the formal power series ring Z[[x]], let (n_k)_{k>=1} be the unique sequence of integers defined by the power-product expansion sum_{n>=0} p(n)x^n = product_{k>=1} (1 + n_k x^k). The paper notes that n_k = 1 for every odd k. Explore the arithmetic properties of the sequence (n_k); in particular, is it true that, for every integer k >= 1, one has n_{8k} > 0 and n_{8k+2}, n_{8k+4}, n_{8k+6} < 0?
justification: This draft is aiming at the paper's Section 2, Problem 3 (page 3), not at any other open problem in the note. The only refinements needed were to make the question fully stand-alone and paper-faithful by adding the formal-power-series setting Z[[x]], making uniqueness and indexing explicit, and incorporating the nearby contextual fact from the same section that n_k = 1 for odd k. I did not broaden the question beyond the paper's own Problem 3.
